exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 1 and 2, find the vector $$\mathbf{x}$$ determined by the given coordinate vector $$\lbrack\textbf{x}\rbrack_{B}$$ and the given basis $$B$$ ﻿. Illustrate your answer with a figure, as in the solution of Practice Problem 2.

problem.paragraph: $$B = \begin{Bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ - 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{Bmatrix} , \left([ \textbf{x} ]\right)_{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$$
$$B = \begin{Bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} - 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{Bmatrix} , \left([ \textbf{x} ]\right)_{B} = \begin{bmatrix} - 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$$

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 3–6, the vector $$\mathbf{x}$$ is in a subspace $$H$$ with a basis $$B = \{\textbf{b}_{1},{}\textbf{b}_{2}\}.$$ Find the $$B \text{-coordinate}$$ vector of $$\mathbf{x}$$ .

problem.paragraph: $$\textbf{b}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ - 4 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{b}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} - 2 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} - 3 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}$$
$$\textbf{b}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ - 3 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{b}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} - 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} - 7 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$$
$$\textbf{b}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \\ - 3 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{b}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} - 3 \\ - 7 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 10 \\ - 7 \end{bmatrix}$$
$$\textbf{b}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} - 3 \\ 1 \\ - 4 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{b}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ 5 \\ - 6 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 11 \\ 0 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}$$

Let $$\textbf{b}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack,\textbf{b}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack,\textbf{w} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 7 \\ {- 2} \end{array} \right\rbrack,\textbf{x} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 4 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack,$$ and $$B = \{\textbf{b}_{1},{}\textbf{b}_{2}\}.$$ Use the figure to estimate $$\lbrack\textbf{w}\rbrack_{B}$$ and $$\lbrack\textbf{x}\rbrack_{B}.$$ Confirm your estimate of $$\lbrack\textbf{x}\rbrack_{B}$$ by using it and $$\{\textbf{b}_{1},{}\textbf{b}_{2}\}$$ to compute $$\mathbf{x}$$ .

Let $$\mathbf{b}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix},\mathbf{b}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix},\mathbf{x} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 2} \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack,\mathbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 4 \end{array} \right\rbrack,\mathbf{z} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ {- 2.5} \end{array} \right\rbrack,$$ and $$B = \{\textbf{b}_{1},{}\textbf{b}_{2}\}.$$ Use the figure to estimate $${\lbrack\textbf{x}\rbrack_{B}},\lbrack\textbf{y}\rbrack_{B},$$ and $$\lbrack\textbf{z}\rbrack_{B}.$$ Confirm your estimates of $$\lbrack\textbf{y}\rbrack_{B}$$ and $$\lbrack\textbf{z}\rbrack_{B}$$ by using them and $$\{\textbf{b}_{1},{}\textbf{b}_{2}\}$$ to compute $$\mathbf{y}$$ and $$\mathbf{z}$$ .

exercise_group.instruction: Exercises 9–12 display a matrix $$A$$ and an echelon form of $$A$$ ﻿. Find bases for Col $$A$$ and Nul $$A$$ ﻿, and then state the dimensions of these subspaces.
In Exercises 13 and 14, find a basis for the subspace spanned by the given vectors. What is the dimension of the subspace?

problem.paragraph: $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ - 3 \\ 2 \\ - 4 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} - 3 \\ 9 \\ - 6 \\ 12 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ - 1 \\ 4 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} - 4 \\ 5 \\ - 3 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}$$

$$\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ - 1 \\ - 2 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ - 3 \\ - 1 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \\ - 6 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} - 1 \\ 4 \\ - 7 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ - 8 \\ 9 \\ - 5 \end{bmatrix}$$
Suppose a $$3 \times 5$$ matrix $$A$$ has three pivot columns. Is Col $$\textit{A} = \mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ ? Is Nul $$\textit{A} = \mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ ? Explain your answers.
Suppose a $$4 \times 7$$ matrix $$A$$ has three pivot columns. Is Col $$\textit{A} = \mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ ? What is the dimension of Nul $$A$$ ? Explain your answers.

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 17–26, mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer. Here $$A$$ is an $$m \times n$$ matrix.

problem.paragraph: (T/F) If $$B = \{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}\}$$ is a basis for a subspace $$H$$ and if $$\textbf{x} = c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + c_{p}\textbf{v}_{p},$$ then $$c_{1},\ldots,c_{p}$$ are the coordinates of $$\textbf{x}$$ relative to the basis $$B$$ .﻿
(T/F) If $$B$$ is a basis for a subspace $$H,$$ then each vector in $$H$$ can be written in only one way as a linear combination of the vectors in $$B$$ .﻿
(T/F) Each line in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ is a one-dimensional subspace of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ .﻿

(T/F) If $$B = \{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}\}$$ is a basis for a subspace $$H$$ of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , then the correspondence $$\textbf{x}\mapsto\lbrack\textbf{x}\rbrack_{B}$$ makes $$H$$ look and act the same as $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{p}$$ .﻿
(T/F) The dimension of Col $$A$$ is the number of pivot columns of $$A$$ .﻿
(T/F) The dimension of Nul $$A$$ is the number of variables in the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ .﻿
(T/F) The dimensions of Col $$A$$ and Nul $$A$$ add up to the number of columns of $$A$$ .﻿
(T/F) The dimension of the column space of $$A$$ is rank $$A$$ .﻿
(T/F) If a set of $$p$$ vectors spans a $$p$$ -dimensional subspace $$H$$ of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , then these vectors form a basis for $$H$$ .﻿
(T/F) If $$H$$ is a $$p$$ -dimensional subspace of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , then a linearly independent set of $$p$$ vectors in $$H$$ is a basis for $$H$$ .﻿

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 27–32, justify each answer or construction.

problem.paragraph: If the subspace of all solutions of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ has a basis consisting of three vectors and if $$A$$ is a $$5 \times 7$$ matrix, what is the rank of $$A$$ ?
What is the rank of a $$4 \times 5$$ matrix whose null space is three-dimensional?
If the rank of a $$7 \times 6$$ matrix $$A$$ is $$4$$ , what is the dimension of the solution space of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ ?

Show that a set of vectors $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{5}\}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ is linearly dependent when dim Span $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{5}\} = 4$$ .﻿
If possible, construct a $$3 \times 4$$ matrix $$A$$ such that dim Nul $$A = 2$$ and dim Col $$A = 2$$ .
Construct a $$4 \times 3$$ matrix with rank $$l$$ .
Let $$A$$ be an $$n \times p$$ matrix whose column space is $$p$$ -dimensional. Explain why the columns of $$A$$ must be linearly independent.

Suppose columns $$1$$ , $$3$$ , $$5$$ , and $$6$$ of a matrix $$A$$ are linearly independent (but are not necessarily pivot columns) and the rank of $$A$$ is $$4$$ . Explain why the four columns mentioned must be a basis for the column space of $$A$$ .﻿

Suppose vectors $$\textbf{b}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{b}_{\textit{p}}$$ span a subspace $$W$$ , and let $$\{\textbf{a}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{a}_{\textit{q}}\}$$ be any set in $$W$$ containing more than $$p$$ vectors. Fill in the details of the following argument to show that $$\{\textbf{a}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{a}_{q}\}$$ must be linearly dependent. First, let $$B = \lbrack\textbf{b}_{1} \cdots \textbf{b}_{p}\rbrack$$ and $$A = \lbrack\textbf{a}_{1} \cdots \textbf{a}_{q}\rbrack$$ .﻿

list.item: Explain why for each vector $$\textbf{a}_{j},$$ there exists a vector $$\textbf{c}_{j}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{p}$$ such that $$\textbf{a}_{j} = B\textbf{c}_{j}$$ .﻿
Let $$C = \lbrack\textbf{c}_{1} \cdots \textbf{c}_{q}\rbrack$$ . Explain why there is a nonzero vector $$\mathbf{u}$$ such that $$C\textbf{u} = \textbf{0}$$ .﻿
Use $$B$$ and $$C$$ to show that $$A\textbf{u} = \textbf{0}$$ . This shows that the columns of $$A$$ are linearly dependent.

problem.paragraph: Use Exercise 35 to show that if $$A$$ and $$B$$ are bases for a subspace $$W$$ of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , then $$A$$ cannot contain more vectors than $$B$$ , and, conversely, $$B$$ cannot contain more vectors than $$A$$ .﻿

[T] Let $$H = \text{Span} \{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2}\}$$ and $$B = \left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2} \right\}$$ . Show that $$\mathbf{x}$$ is in $$H,$$ and find the $$\textit{B} \text{-coordinate}$$ vector of $$\mathbf{x}$$ , when $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 11 \\ - 5 \\ 10 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 14 \\ - 8 \\ 13 \\ 10 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 19 \\ - 13 \\ 18 \\ 15 \end{bmatrix}$$

[T] Let $$H = { \text{S} \text{p} \text{a} \text{n} }\{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3}\}$$ and $$B = \left\{ {\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2},\mathbf{v}_{3}} \right\}.$$ Show that $$B$$ is a basis for $$H$$ and $$\mathbf{x}$$ is in $$H$$ , and find the $$\textit{B} \text{-coordinate}$$ vector of $$\mathbf{x}$$ , when $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} - 6 \\ 4 \\ - 9 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 \\ - 3 \\ 7 \\ - 3 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} - 9 \\ 5 \\ - 8 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 7 \\ - 8 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$$

problem.paragraph: Construct $$A = \lbrack\textbf{v}_{1} \textbf{v}_{2} \textbf{v}_{3}\rbrack$$ so that the subspace spanned by $$\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3}$$ is the column space of $$A$$ . A basis for this space is provided by the pivot columns of $$A$$ .﻿ $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & - 1 \\ - 8 & - 7 & 6 \\ 6 & - 1 & - 7 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & - 1 \\ 0 & 5 & 2 \\ 0 & - 10 & - 4 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & - 1 \\ 0 & 5 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$
The first two columns of $$A$$ are pivot columns and form a basis for $$H$$ . Thus $$\dim H = 2.$$

If $$\left\lbrack \textbf{x} \right\rbrack_{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix},$$ then $$\textbf{x}$$ is formed from a linear combination of the basis vectors using weights $$3$$ and $$2$$ : $$\textbf{x} = 3 \textbf{b}_{1} + 2 \textbf{b}_{2} = 3 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ .2 \end{bmatrix} + 2 \begin{bmatrix} .2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3.4 \\ 2.6 \end{bmatrix}$$

The basis $$\{\textbf{b}_{1},\textbf{b}_{2}\}$$ determines a coordinate system for $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ , illustrated by the grid in the figure. Note how $$\textbf{x}$$ is $$3$$ units in the $$\textbf{b}_{1} \text{-direction}$$ and $$2$$ units in the $$\textbf{b}_{2} \text{-direction}$$ .

A four-dimensional subspace would contain a basis of four linearly independent vectors. This is impossible inside $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}.$$ Since any linearly independent set in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ has no more than three vectors, any subspace of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ has dimension no more than $$3$$ . The space $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ itself is the only three-dimensional subspace of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ . Other subspaces of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ have dimension $$2$$ , $$1$$ , or $$0$$ .
